paper1_text: Inexperienced researchers often lack knowledge of the implicit writing conventions and structural expectations of particular communities. While existing writing guides offer general advice, they are often too abstract and high-level, making it challenging for junior researchers to apply this guidance in their own work.

None of the paper2 candidate paragraphs address this topic at all; they instead motivate a completely different problem about learning to use software APIs, code examples, and the EXAMPLORE tool. There is no thematic overlap between the query's subject (research writing conventions) and any candidate (API usage learning, code mining, visualization tools). Thus no paragraph corresponds.

paper1_text: Given that people commonly learn through examples, providing access to relevant examples can help bridge this gap. However, there are obstacles: viewing too few examples may lead to overfitting and unintentional plagiarism, while viewing too many examples—without sufficient cognitive supports within the interface—may overwhelm the writer.
paper2_text: Code-sharing sites like GitHub hold the promise of documenting all the common and uncommon ways of using an API in practice, including many alternative usage scenarios that are not typically shown in curated examples. However, given the large amount of code available online, it is challenging for developers to efficiently browse the enormous volume of search results. It is certainly infeasible for developers to examine more than a few code examples simultaneously. In practice, programmers often investigate a handful of search results and return to their own code due to limited time and attention [3, 23, 5]. Prior work has shown that individual code examples may suffer from API usage violations [29], insecure coding practices [7], unchecked obsolete usage [31], and comprehension difficulties [25]. Therefore, inspecting a few examples may leave out critical safety checks or desirable usage scenarios.
basis: The query paragraph discusses the tension in providing examples: too few examples risks overfitting/plagiarism, too many overwhelms the reader without cognitive support. This closely parallels paragraph [2], which discusses the challenge that inspecting only a few code examples 'may leave out critical safety checks or desirable usage scenarios' (too few examples), while also noting 'given the large amount of code available online, it is challenging for developers to efficiently browse the enormous volume of search results' and 'infeasible for developers to examine more than a few code examples simultaneously' (too many examples overwhelming). Both paragraphs articulate the same two-sided obstacle—insufficient examples vs. overwhelming volume—motivating the need for a better interface/tool to support example-based learning.

paper1_text: Prior work motivated the design of writing support tools with social cognitive theories and cognitive apprenticeship theory [18, 19] to help writers learn complex writing skills in a professional setting. While this approach allows novices to learn by mimicking model examples, it also requires expert knowledge to create and annotate these examples, which is often time-consuming and not readily available for many communities.
paper2_text: One study found that the greatest obstacle to learning an API is "insufficient or inadequate examples." [19] Official documentation is typically dominated by textual descriptions and explanations, often lacking concrete code examples that illustrate API usage. Tutorials and blog posts walk developers through simplified code examples but often without demonstrating alternative uses of an API, which programmers frequently desire when learning unfamiliar APIs [5, 19, 4].
basis: The query paragraph discusses a limitation of prior theory-driven writing support tools: they rely on expert-created model examples that are time-consuming to produce and not readily available. This closely parallels paper2's paragraph [1], which discusses how learning APIs suffers from 'insufficient or inadequate examples,' noting that official documentation lacks concrete examples and tutorials often don't show alternative uses. Both paragraphs identify the core problem as a shortage of good, expert-curated examples for learners in their respective domains (writing skills vs. API usage), motivating the need for new example-generation/visualization approaches. While not identical in domain, this is the closest thematic counterpart discussing the scarcity/cost of quality examples as the core motivating limitation.

paper1_text: Learning from examples has also been extensively covered in the language learning literature. Non-native English speakers (NNES) may hesitate to choose from AI-suggested content because they struggle to evaluate the content's fluency and naturalness [21, 24, 25]. To address this problem, researchers proposed that novices learn by inspecting sentences from a curated corpus such as the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) or English dictionaries [4] to help students learn the correct use of collocations and phrases [35]. To this end, LangSmith proposed a writing support tool for drafting academic NLP papers [20] by generating grammatically correct phrases given the user's current draft along with prior section and paper titles. In contrast, our work surfaces existing text from a relevant peer-reviewed text corpus. Furthermore, by avoiding automatically generated text that may—without the writer's knowledge—cross the line into plagiarism if used verbatim, the writer only sees previously published example sentences and their provenance, retaining informed control.
basis: The query paragraph discusses example-based language learning literature (NNES writers, COCA corpus, LangSmith academic writing tool) and contrasts the paper's approach (surfacing existing peer-reviewed text without plagiarism risk) to that prior work. None of the paper2 candidates address language learning, writing support tools, or NNES writers—they instead focus on API usage learning challenges, code examples, Big Code mining, and the EXAMPLORE visualization tool. There is no thematic overlap between this query paragraph's specific domain (writing/language learning tools) and any candidate paragraph in this pool, so no correspondence exists.

paper1_text: To this end, we implemented CorpusStudio, a writing environment with two novel writing support concepts, one at the document level and one at the sentence level, that help writers learn about the writing styles and expectations of particular audiences. These writing supports are designed to expose writers to as many examples as possible to increase the variety of examples shown to the users—with the cognitive support necessary to help them see the emergent patterns that capture otherwise implicit community-specific writing content and style expectations. Specifically, at the document level, CorpusStudio computes and renders an ordered distribution [15] over section title sequences in prior papers from the community the writer wishes to write for. This gives the writer a sense of common and uncommon section titles and in what relative order they appear in prior papers (Figure 1A). At the sentence level, CorpusStudio retrieves many example sentences from the corpus given the user's draft-in-progress and their current cursor location within it (Figure 1C). Words across these many example sentences are algorithmically highlighted or de-emphasized to help users see any emergent norms and outliers. We also allow authors to capture their thoughts and deductions from viewing these examples with bookmarks and notes.
paper2_text: In this paper, we introduce a novel interactive visualization and navigation technique called EXAMPLORE that (1) gives a bird's-eye view of common and uncommon ways in which a community of developers uses an API and (2) allows developers to quickly filter a corpus for concrete code examples that exhibit these various uses. It operates on hundreds of code examples of a given API method, which can be automatically mined from open-source projects or proprietary codebases. It is designed to supplement existing resources: for example, while Stack Overflow can provide explanations and discussions, EXAMPLORE provides quantitative information about how an API call is used in the wild.
basis: The query paragraph introduces CorpusStudio, describing its novel writing support tool and its two-level (document and sentence) mechanisms for exposing users to many examples with cognitive support to reveal patterns. This parallels candidate [4], which introduces EXAMPLORE as the novel tool of that paper, describing its two main capabilities: giving a bird's-eye view of common/uncommon API usage (distributional/statistical view) and allowing drill-down into concrete supporting examples. Both paragraphs serve the same structural role of introducing the paper's central tool/system and its high-level dual capabilities, right after motivating the problem. While paragraph [5] elaborates further mechanistic detail (skeleton, filtering), [4] is the closer match as the initial 'introduce the tool' paragraph analogous to the query's introduction of CorpusStudio.

paper1_text: We conducted a user study with N=16 participants from the academic community who were actively writing their manuscripts. They used CorpusStudio to draft their paper outline, wrote one to two sections of their manuscript, and answered questionnaires eliciting their overall experience writing within CorpusStudio.
paper2_text: We conducted a within-subjects lab study where we asked sixteen Java programmers of various levels of expertise to answer questions about the usage of particular Java APIs based on either (1) searching online for relevant code examples, blogs, and forum posts or (2) using EXAMPLORE to explore one hundred API usage examples mined from GitHub. On average, participants answered significantly more API usage questions correctly, with more concrete details, using EXAMPLORE. This suggests that EXAMPLORE helps users grasp a more comprehensive view of API usage than online search. In a post survey, the majority of participants (13/16) found EXAMPLORE to be more helpful for answering API usage questions than online search, and when using EXAMPLORE, their median level of confidence in their answers was higher.
basis: The query describes a user study (N=16 participants) evaluating the tool (CorpusStudio) via a task and questionnaires eliciting experience. Candidate [6] similarly describes the user study conducted for EXAMPLORE (sixteen Java programmers) evaluating the tool's effectiveness, including a post survey/questionnaire eliciting participant experience and confidence. Both paragraphs serve the same role: reporting the user study setup/participants and outcome in the introduction. Other candidates (0-5,7) discuss motivation, tool description, or contributions rather than the study itself, so [6] is the closest match despite paper1's paragraph being more about study procedure and paper2's being more about study findings.

paper1_text: Our results reveal that users felt more confident in their writing when they discovered that other people in their target community have written in a similar way. Inspecting many examples at once was useful for identifying broad structural patterns, especially for sections that typically have more common structure, such as the description of the system implementation details or participants' demographics.

On average, participants answered significantly more API usage questions correctly, with more concrete details, using EXAMPLORE. This suggests that EXAMPLORE helps users grasp a more comprehensive view of API usage than online search. In a post survey, the majority of participants (13/16) found EXAMPLORE to be more helpful for answering API usage questions than online search, and when using EXAMPLORE, their median level of confidence in their answers was higher.

paper1_text: In summary, we contribute the following: • We designed two novel writing support concepts that make visible emergent patterns at the document-level and sentence-level of a given paper corpus. • We implemented these writing support concepts within CorpusStudio, an interactive writing environment that helps writers retrieve, inspect, generalize from, and reflect on many examples from their target venue • We found that users' writing goals guided their perception of relevance and how they adapted content from the corpus.
paper2_text: Our contributions are: • a method for generating an interactive visualization of a distribution of code examples for a given API call • an implementation of this interactive visualization for a set of Java and Android API calls • a within-subjects lab study that shows how this interactive visualization may fill an important role in developers' programming workflows as they use unfamiliar APIs.
basis: Both paragraphs are the "contributions" list at the end of the Introduction, summarizing what the paper delivers: paper1 lists design concepts, an implemented tool (CorpusStudio), and a study finding; paper2 lists a visualization method, an implementation (EXAMPLORE) for Java/Android APIs, and a lab study finding. This is a direct structural and functional match, unlike earlier paragraphs which discuss motivation/problem framing rather than contributions.
